title: Southwest Airlines 1380

agencies.name: Bureau d'Enquêtes et d'Analyses pour la Sécurité de l'Aviation Civile

summary: Southwest Airlines Boeing 737-700 experienced catastrophic left engine failure at 32,000 feet 30 minutes after departure from LaGuardia. A latent fatigue crack in fan blade No. 13 caused the blade to detach and strike the engine case at a critical location, causing fan cowl latch failure and separation. Engine debris damaged the leading edge of the wing and broke a cabin window at row 14, causing explosive decompression. The aircraft descended and diverted to Philadelphia International Airport. One passenger was partially ejected and died; eight others sustained minor injuries.
probable_cause: A low-cycle fatigue crack in the dovetail of fan blade No. 13 resulted in the fan blade separating in flight and impacting the engine fan case at a location critical to the structural integrity of the fan cowl structure. This impact led to the in-flight separation of fan cowl components, including the inboard fan cowl aft latch keeper, which struck the fuselage near a cabin window and caused the window to depart from the airplane, the cabin to rapidly depressurize, and the passenger fatality.

factors.evidence: a low-cycle fatigue crack in the dovetail of fan blade No. 13 caused the blade to detach from the fan disk (p. 462)

the detached blade fragment struck the fan case at the six o'clock position; although it did not penetrate the case, the impact caused the cowling latch to fail and engine cowling to detach (p. 462-463)

the impact of the separated fan blade with the fan case imparted significant loads into the fan cowl through the radial restraint fitting, causing cracks that propagated forward and aft, severing three latch assemblies (p. 462)
the inboard fan cowl aft latch keeper struck the fuselage near the cabin window at row 14, breaking the window and causing rapid depressurization (p. 462)
the aircraft rolled to the left by 41.3° as a result of the engine failure and structural damage (p. 690-691)

events.text: Fan blade No. 13 in left CFM56-7B engine fractured due to low-cycle fatigue crack at the dovetail
Cabin altitude warning horn activated; cabin altitude exceeded 10,000 ft due to window breach
Aircraft uncommanded left roll reached maximum of 41.3°
Pilot flying (first officer) began emergency descent; right engine power reduced to idle
Left engine fuel cutoff; engine began windmilling
Aircraft landed successfully at Philadelphia International Airport runway 27L

recommendations.text: Require Boeing to determine the critical fan blade impact location(s) on the CFM56-7B engine fan case and redesign the fan cowl structure on all Boeing 737 next-generation-series airplanes to ensure the structural integrity of the fan cowl after a fan-blade-out event
Once the actions requested in Safety Recommendation A-19-17 are completed, require Boeing to install the redesigned fan cowl structure on new-production 737 next-generation-series airplanes

Once the actions requested in Safety Recommendation A-19-17 are completed, require operators of Boeing 737 next-generation-series airplanes to retrofit their airplanes with the redesigned fan cowl structure

Expand the Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 25 and 33 certification requirements to mandate that airplane and engine manufacturers work collaboratively to analyze all critical fan blade impact locations for all engine operating conditions, the resulting fan blade fragmentation, and the effects of the fan-blade-out-generated loads on the nacelle structure
Develop and issue guidance on ways that air carriers can mitigate hazards to passengers affected by an in-flight loss of seating capacity

Include the lessons learned from the accident involving Southwest Airlines flight 1380 in initial and recurrent flight attendant training, emphasizing the importance of being secured in a jumpseat during emergency landings

Expand your certification requirements for transport-category airplanes and aircraft engines to mandate that airplane and engine manufacturers work collaboratively to analyze all critical fan blade impact locations for all engine operating conditions, the resulting fan blade fragmentation, and the effects of the fan-blade-out-generated loads on the nacelle structure

safety_changes: CFM developed eddy current inspection (ECI) procedure for fan blades at overhaul to detect subsurface cracks
CFM developed on-wing ultrasonic inspection technique for fan blade relubrication to detect cracks before critical failure
FAA and EASA issued multiple airworthiness directives requiring enhanced fan blade inspections on CFM56-7B engines

notes: Sections read: Executive Summary (p. viii), History of Flight (p. 644-843), Findings (p. 4406-4464), Probable Cause (p. 4465-4472), Recommendations (p. 4479-4511)
